q: An employee's bank details change on the 27th, two days after the payroll input cut-off. What should happen to this month's salary?
o: Pay to the account on file; apply the new details next run once verified
Hold the salary until the new account is verified and loaded in the system
Pay to the new account, as the employee's latest instruction takes priority
Split the payment between the old and new accounts for this month only
e: Late bank-detail changes are a common fraud route. Paying the verified account on file keeps the employee paid on time; the change is verified and applied next cycle.

q: Which document is the strongest source for an employee's salary when payroll and the HRIS disagree?
o: The latest signed contract or approved salary change
The amount paid consistently over the last three months
The figure the line manager confirms in writing by email
The HRIS value, because the HRIS is the system of record
e: Payroll and the HRIS are both downstream of the approved instrument. Past payments can repeat an old error, and a manager's email is not an approval of pay.

q: What is the main purpose of a payroll variance report reviewed before each payment run?
o: To explain each material change before money is released
To confirm total payroll cost stays within the annual budget
To give finance the joiners and leavers needed for accruals
To show employees why net pay changed from the last month
e: A variance review is a pre-payment control: every movement must be explained and approved before funds are released.

q: A one-off bonus was approved for 12 employees but the payroll file contains 13. What is the right first step?
o: Stop and reconcile the file to the signed approval list
Process all 13 and recover any excess payment next month
Remove the lowest bonus so the file matches the approval
Pay the 12 matching names now and the 13th next month
e: Payroll must match the approval exactly. Reconciling first shows whether the approval or the file is wrong.

q: In payroll, segregation of duties mainly means:
o: The person who enters changes does not approve or release them
Payroll and HR report to different managers and departments
Each payroll team member looks after a separate employee population
Salary data is held in a separate system from personal data
e: Segregation separates input, approval and release so no single person can create and pay an unauthorised change.

q: Payroll runs on the 20th. A promotion effective from the 1st of the same month is approved and arrives on the 24th. What is the best treatment?
o: Pay the new rate next month with arrears back to the 1st
Change the effective date to next month to avoid arrears
Run an off-cycle payment now for the full new salary
Reverse this month's payroll and rerun it at the new rate
e: The approval sets the effective date, not payroll timing. Arrears in the next regular run preserve it without an off-cycle run or reversal.

q: A salary advance is being recovered monthly. The employee resigns with three instalments outstanding. What should payroll check first?
o: What the signed advance agreement says about early exit
Whether the final settlement is large enough to cover it
Whether the line manager is willing to waive the balance
The standard company practice for final pay deductions
e: Recovery depends on what the employee agreed in writing and on the rules on deductions. The agreement comes first.

q: Gross pay matches the payroll register, but the bank file total is short by exactly one employee's net pay. What is the most likely cause?
o: One employee's payment record is missing from the bank file
A deduction was posted twice for one of the employees
One employee's housing allowance was paid at the wrong monthly rate
Statutory contributions were calculated on the wrong base
e: If gross agrees and the bank total is short by exactly one net pay, a payment record is missing. Rate or deduction errors would also show in the register.

q: Which control is most effective at detecting 'ghost' employees in payroll?
o: Reconciling payroll headcount to HR records and managers
Requiring two signatures on every salary bank payment file
Restricting payroll system access to the payroll team only
Comparing total payroll cost with the previous month's cost
e: Ghost employees look legitimate inside payroll, so signatures and cost trends can miss them. Independent headcount reconciliation exposes them.

q: An employee was overpaid AED 4,000 by mistake three months ago. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Explain the error in writing and agree a recovery plan
Deduct the full amount from next month's salary to close it
Write the amount off, since the error was the company's fault
Recover the amount from the final settlement when they leave
e: Overpayments are generally recoverable, but recovery should be transparent and agreed to avoid hardship or an unlawful deduction.

q: Two months after a new payroll system went live, net pay is correct but GL postings are misallocated between cost centres. Where is the root cause most likely?
o: Cost-centre mapping in the general ledger interface
Configuration of allowance and deduction pay elements
The format of the salary bank transfer file
Contribution or tax tables loaded during implementation
e: Correct net pay means calculations are right. Consistent misallocation points to the mapping between organisational data and accounting.

q: Finance wants salary accruals for the last 10 days of the month because pay is calculated on the 20th. Which data matters most?
o: Approved joiners, leavers and overtime after cut-off
The average monthly payroll cost across the previous quarter
The full payroll register exactly as processed on the 20th
Budgeted headcount and salary cost for the month in question
e: An accrual covers cost incurred but not processed. The register already reflects the cut-off; the gap is approved movements after it.

q: A manager wants a 15% retention allowance for an engineer already paid at 118% of the range midpoint. What is the main risk to raise?
o: Pay drifting well above range and creating equity issues with peers
The allowance being treated as basic salary for all entitlements
The engineer becoming ineligible for this year's annual bonus
The department going over its approved monthly salary budget for the year
e: At 118% of midpoint the employee is already high in range. A further 15% pushes pay far beyond the structure and raises equity questions.

q: The same employee's overtime has been approved every month for a year at exactly 40 hours. What is the best response?
o: Check the timesheets or access logs behind the approvals
Stop the overtime payments until the manager justifies the hours in writing
Accept the approvals, as overtime is the manager's call
Report the manager to internal audit for suspected fraud
e: A flat, unchanging pattern is a red flag, not proof. Checking source evidence is proportionate.

q: A company moves its pay date from the 28th to the 1st of the following month. What is the most important implication to manage?
o: A cash-flow gap for employees in the transition month
Annual leave accruals falling into the wrong pay period
Overtime for the month needing to be recalculated
Year-end payroll reports showing one fewer pay period
e: Moving the pay date later stretches the gap between two pay days. The people impact is cash flow, which needs early notice and often a bridging option.

q: An audit finds six incorrect allowances in a 2,000-person payroll, all entered by one new team member in the same month. What is the best corrective action?
o: Fix the six, retrain, and review that person's inputs for a period
Re-check all 2,000 employees' allowances before the next run
Remove the team member's access to the payroll system for good
Correct the six cases and close the audit finding as resolved
e: The pattern is concentrated, so a targeted fix plus a temporary second review addresses the cause proportionately.

q: One payroll specialist alone understands the final settlement logic and starts extended leave next month. What should be prioritised?
o: Document the logic and have a second person run settlements under supervision
Agree that she stays reachable by phone for urgent settlements during leave
Defer all final settlements until she returns, so the logic stays consistent
Hire a temporary contractor with broad payroll experience to cover her role in full
e: Key-person dependency is resolved by transferring knowledge and proving it works. Phone access or deferral pushes the risk onto leavers.

q: After a merger, two groups in the same role have different allowance structures. Leadership wants one structure with no one losing pay. What is the most workable approach?
o: One structure, with any shortfall protected as a phasing-out personal allowance
Move everyone to the more generous of the two structures with immediate effect
Keep both structures permanently and apply each one by the original legal entity
Move everyone to the lower structure and pay a one-time compensation amount
e: Red-circling the difference protects pay without keeping two structures forever and keeps harmonisation affordable.

q: Audit finds 9% of last year's salary changes were processed before the approval date on the form. Most were approved later. How should payroll respond?
o: Block processing without a dated approval and report the exceptions
Accept the position, since nearly all changes were approved in the end
Ask managers to date approvals to match the payroll processing dates
Add a monthly review of changes processed in the previous month
e: Later approval doesn't repair a failed preventive control. Re-dating approvals would falsify records; an after-the-fact review keeps the gap open.

q: Payroll cost rose 6% in a quarter with no headcount change and no pay review. Which analysis explains it fastest?
o: Variance by pay element and by population mix
Average salary per employee compared with the previous quarter
A market benchmark of total payroll cost for similar companies
A review of the budget assumptions set at the start of the year
e: With headcount and base pay stable, the movement is in variable elements or mix. Element-level analysis locates it.

q: An employee's pay is above the maximum of a new grade range going live next month. What is the most defensible treatment?
o: Keep current pay, red-circle it, and limit increases until the range catches up
Reduce pay to the range maximum after giving three months' written notice
Move the employee up to the next grade so that the current salary fits the range
Exclude the employee from the new structure until they are promoted
e: Red-circling protects pay without distorting grading. Cutting pay risks a contractual claim; regrading for salary fit undermines job evaluation.

q: You are designing payroll controls for a move to bi-weekly pay across three new countries. Which principle matters most?
o: One control set, with statutory steps adapted per country
Let each country team design its own controls to suit local practice
Use a single outsourced provider and rely on its control framework
Prioritise automation so that fewer manual controls are needed
e: A common control spine keeps assurance consistent while allowing legal differences. Outsourcing and automation still need the employer's own controls.

q: A pay equity review finds a 7% unexplained gap for the same roles after controlling for grade, tenure and performance. Budget can close half of it this year. What should you recommend?
o: Close the largest gaps first, set a dated plan for the rest, and fix the cause
Spread the available budget evenly across everyone in the lower-paid group
Wait until next year so the full gap can be closed in a single step
Re-run the analysis with additional controls until the gap is explained
e: Targeting the largest individual gaps reduces the worst inequity first; a dated plan and process fix prevent recurrence. Adding controls until a gap disappears is a known way to hide it.

q: Leadership wants to cut payroll cost by 5% without redundancies. Which option generally preserves the most long-term value?
o: Review overtime, allowances and contractor spend first
Apply a 5% salary cut to all employees above a set grade
Freeze all pay increases and promotions for two years
Convert part of everyone's fixed pay into a bonus
e: Variable and structural costs can often be reduced with less damage to retention and trust than across-the-board cuts or long freezes.

q: Two years after a payroll system implementation, manual adjustments still make up 12% of each run. What is the strongest next step?
o: Group the adjustments by root cause and fix the main drivers
Limit manual adjustments to senior payroll staff only
Replace the system, as it is not meeting business needs
Add a second reviewer to sign off every manual adjustment
e: Persistent manual adjustments are a symptom. A few causes usually drive most of them; extra reviewers or a new system don't remove the cause.

q: An employee asks HR to correct their date of birth in the HRIS. What is required before the change?
o: An official identity document showing the correct date
Written approval of the change from the line manager
A signed declaration from the employee confirming it
Confirmation from payroll that pay will not be affected
e: Identity data must match an official document. Approvals and declarations don't prove the fact.

q: What is the main purpose of a service-level agreement (SLA) for HR requests?
o: To set measurable response and resolution times
To limit how many requests each employee can raise
To describe each HR team member's responsibilities
To make sure an HR manager approves every request
e: An SLA defines expected service levels so performance can be measured and improved.

q: An HR team keeps signed contracts in personal email folders. What is the most important risk?
o: Uncontrolled access and unreliable retrieval of records
Mailbox storage limits being exceeded as files build up
Employees being unable to view their own contracts
Contracts being signed by the wrong level of manager
e: Personal folders break access control, retention and audit trails, which are the core purposes of records management.

q: An onboarding checklist step is skipped repeatedly because it takes too long. What should the process owner do first?
o: Check whether the step is still needed and why it is slow
Make the step mandatory and report who keeps skipping it
Remove the step from the checklist to save everyone time
Ask the HR director to remind the team to complete it
e: Repeated skipping signals a design problem. Understanding purpose and obstacle comes before enforcing or removing the step.

q: Employee files are kept indefinitely 'just in case'. Why is this a problem?
o: Keeping data past its purpose raises privacy risk
It uses up too much storage space in the HR system
It makes older employee files harder to search
It slows down onboarding for newly hired employees
e: Data protection principles require retention tied to a purpose and period. 'Just in case' is not a retention basis.

q: Two HR policies give different notice periods for the same group. An employee resigns. What should HR apply?
o: The contract term, then fix the conflicting policies
The longer notice period, to protect the business
The shorter notice period, as it favours the employee
The notice period in the most recently issued policy
e: The contract is the primary agreement with the employee. The policy conflict is a separate governance fix.

q: HR queries are resolved within SLA, but satisfaction with HR service keeps falling. What should be examined next?
o: Reopened cases and the quality of the answers given
Whether the SLA response targets are set too generously
The number of agents in the HR shared-services team
The volume of queries raised per employee each month
e: Fast but poor answers create repeat contacts. Quality and first-contact resolution explain satisfaction better than speed.

q: A manager asks HR to email his team's salary spreadsheet to his personal address to work from home. What should HR do?
o: Decline and offer secure access through company channels
Send it password-protected, as he can already see the data
Send it after removing employee names from the spreadsheet
Send it and ask him to delete the file once he has finished
e: Authorisation to view data doesn't authorise moving it into uncontrolled personal accounts.

q: An audit finds 14% of leavers still had system access 30 days after exit. Which fix addresses the root cause?
o: Trigger access removal from the HR exit record
Send IT a monthly list of leavers for access removal
Ask managers to confirm removal in the exit checklist
Run a quarterly access review across all key systems
e: Manual hand-offs and periodic reviews leave gaps. Linking removal to the authoritative HR event closes them at source.

q: You are asked to cut onboarding cycle time from offer acceptance to day one. Which analysis comes first?
o: Map the end-to-end flow with hand-offs and waiting times
Benchmark the cycle time against competitors in the same sector
Survey recent joiners about their onboarding experience
Review the onboarding policy for steps that are outdated
e: Most cycle time sits in waiting between hand-offs. Mapping the flow shows where.

q: A new HR policy was approved, but employees keep applying the old rule. What is the most likely gap?
o: Systems, forms and manager guidance still reflect the old rule
The new policy wording is too long and too complex to follow
Employees did not read the announcement email when it was sent
Managers personally disagree with the change in the policy
e: People follow the tools in front of them. If forms and systems still reflect the old rule, the new policy exists only on paper.

q: An employee asks for a copy of all personal data HR holds about them. What is the best first step?
o: Verify their identity and log the request with its deadline
Ask the employee to explain why they need a copy of the data
Send the full personnel file straight away to show openness
Ask the line manager whether the request should be fulfilled
e: Access requests generally need no reason. Identity checks and tracking the deadline come first; sending data unchecked risks disclosure to the wrong person.

q: A simple address change needs four approvals and takes nine days. What principle should guide the redesign?
o: Match the level of approval to the risk of the change
Keep all four approvals but run them in parallel
Remove all approvals and rely on a later audit check
Route all four approvals to one senior HR manager
e: Controls should be proportionate. A low-risk change needs validation, not four approvers.

q: HR wants to automate offer letters. There are 23 template variants maintained by different people. What should happen before automation?
o: Reduce to a governed, owned template set, then automate
Automate all 23 variants so the business is not disrupted
Choose a vendor tool and let it define the templates
Automate the three most used variants and keep the rest
e: Automating an uncontrolled process scales its inconsistency. Standardise and assign ownership first.

q: A compliance review finds a mandatory registration step was missed for 40 employees over two years. What is the best order of actions?
o: Correct the cases, assess exposure, report it, then fix the process
Fix the process first so no new cases occur, then clear the backlog
Report to leadership and wait for a decision before correcting anything
Correct the cases quietly to avoid attention on the original error
e: Correcting cases reduces ongoing exposure fastest; transparency and the root-cause fix follow. Concealment creates bigger legal and trust risk.

q: An HR service centre handles 6,000 tickets a month; 35% are 'where is my letter' follow-ups. What is the most effective fix?
o: Visible request tracking plus automated standard letters
More agents so follow-up tickets are answered faster
A rule that follow-up tickets will not be answered
A longer service-level target for all standard letter requests
e: Follow-ups are failure demand caused by lack of visibility. Removing the cause beats handling it faster.

q: You inherit a 180-page HR policy manual that managers say they never use. What will most improve compliance?
o: Rebuild it around tasks, with short rules and named owners
Add a detailed index and search to the existing manual
Require every manager to sign that they have read it in full
Summarise the manual on a one-page poster for offices
e: Usability drives compliance. Task-based guidance with owners gets used; sign-offs and posters don't change behaviour.

q: The board asks for assurance that HR compliance is effective across five countries. What should the assurance rest on?
o: A risk-based control register with owners and testing evidence
Annual self-certification letters from each country HR head
An external audit of the largest country every single year
A dashboard of mandatory policy training completion rates
e: Assurance needs evidence that key controls operate. Self-certification and training completion are inputs, not proof.

q: An operating model review finds HR business partners spend half their time on transactional queries. Which change fixes the root cause?
o: A tiered service model that routes transactional work elsewhere
Hiring more HR business partners so they can absorb the query volume
A rule that HR business partners must not answer such queries
Fewer HR policies, so that fewer queries are raised overall
e: Without a channel for transactional work, it flows to whoever is accessible. A tiered model redirects it structurally.

q: A regulator introduces a new employment requirement effective in 60 days. What is the strongest implementation approach?
o: Gap analysis, named owners, system changes and communication
Wait for the official FAQs before starting any of the work
Issue a policy update now and handle questions as they come
Ask external counsel to run the whole implementation for you
e: Implementation needs a structured gap analysis and change plan. Waiting compresses the timeline, and a policy alone doesn't change systems or practice.

q: Process mining shows 30% of internal transfers bypass the documented workflow. What should you conclude first?
o: The workflow may not fit real needs, so find out why
Employees are avoiding controls and need disciplining
The system needs hard restrictions to block bypassing
The data is probably wrong because 30% is too high
e: High bypass rates usually reveal a design mismatch. Understanding why comes before enforcement.

q: A new joiner arrives on day one with no laptop or system access. What does this most clearly show?
o: Pre-boarding tasks were not triggered or tracked in time
The new joiner did not confirm the agreed start date
IT lacks enough staff to support onboarding requests
The line manager is not engaged enough with the new hire
e: Day-one readiness depends on tasks triggered at offer acceptance and tracked to completion.

q: What is the main purpose of an exit interview?
o: To learn why people leave and act on the patterns
To persuade the employee to withdraw the resignation
To confirm the employee's final settlement amount
To collect company property before the last day
e: Exit interviews are a feedback tool; their value comes from aggregating themes and acting on them.

q: A probation review is due next week, but the manager never set objectives. What should HR advise?
o: Review against the role's core expectations and record the gap
Confirm the employee automatically, as no objectives were set
Extend probation until there are objectives to measure against
Postpone the review until the manager has set clear objectives
e: The review can still assess the role's core expectations. Automatic confirmation or postponement creates risk; the missing objectives need fixing either way.

q: Which is the strongest sign that onboarding is working?
o: New hires reach target productivity on time and stay
All onboarding checklist items are completed on time
New joiners give the welcome session consistently high ratings
The induction covers every department in the company
e: Completion and satisfaction are inputs. Time to productivity and early retention show the outcome.

q: A manager wants to confirm an employee at the end of probation, but performance is borderline. Policy allows one extension. What is the best advice?
o: Extend once, with measurable expectations and a decision date
Confirm now and manage the performance issues afterwards
End the employment now, since the standard is not being fully met
Extend the probation period while keeping the same objectives
e: A defined extension gives a fair chance with clarity. Confirming without addressing the gap stores up a harder problem.

q: An internal transfer is approved, but the current manager wants to delay the move by three months. What is the best HR position?
o: Agree a reasonable handover period and protect the move
Support the current manager, as continuity comes first
Move the employee at once and let the old team adapt to the gap
Let the employee decide when they would like to move
e: Blocking internal moves discourages mobility. A defined handover balances both needs.

q: Exit interviews show 'better salary' as the top reason for leaving. How should this be read?
o: As a lead to test against pay data and other likely causes
As a clear signal to raise salaries for the affected roles now
As noise, since most leavers give salary as their reason anyway
As a reason to benchmark every role in the company to market
e: Pay is often the easy reason to give. Validate it with compa-ratios and look for co-occurring drivers such as the manager.

q: A resigning employee asks to use remaining annual leave instead of working the notice period. What should HR check first?
o: What the contract and leave policy allow, and approval
Whether the manager would prefer them to leave early
Whether the leave balance exactly equals the notice
Whether all of the handover documentation is already complete
e: Leave during notice depends on contract, policy and approval. Balance and handover are secondary.

q: An employee returns from long-term sick leave with medical advice for a phased return. The manager needs a full-time person now. What is the best approach?
o: Agree a phased plan per the advice, with set review points
Require a full-time return or extend sick leave until fit
Accept the phased return but keep the full workload as is
Bring in a temporary hire and pause the return to work
e: A structured phased return supports recovery and reduces relapse risk. Forcing full-time work or keeping the full workload defeats the medical advice.

q: Early attrition (leavers within six months) has doubled in one function. Which data would best locate the cause?
o: Patterns by hiring manager, source and role, plus leaver feedback
Company-wide engagement survey scores for the current and previous year
Annual turnover rates for the whole company over five years
Up-to-date salary benchmarks for every role in the function
e: Early attrition usually traces to selection, expectations or the manager. Segmenting by those factors locates it.

q: A high performer resigns and a counter-offer is under discussion. What is the strongest reason for caution?
o: It rarely fixes the reason for leaving and sets a pay precedent
Counter-offers are not allowed once a resignation is submitted
The employee is likely to ask for a promotion at the same time
The manager may already have identified a suitable replacement
e: If the reason was not pay, money doesn't solve it, and visible counter-offers encourage others to resign for a raise.

q: A company plans to move 80 employees to a new office 40 km away. What should HR assess first?
o: Contract terms on place of work and the impact on people
The cost of providing transport for all affected staff
Whether each affected employee is willing to make the move
The timeline for vacating the current office building
e: Contractual place-of-work terms decide what can be required. Individual impact then shapes support and risk.

q: A restructure will close a team of 12. Six similar roles exist elsewhere. What is the fairest way to fill them?
o: Objective criteria applied consistently, after consultation
Offer the six roles to the longest-serving members of the closing team
Let the receiving managers choose who they want to take
Offer the roles to the six best performers from last year
e: Single-factor selection or manager preference is hard to defend. Objective, consistent criteria and consultation protect fairness.

q: Onboarding NPS is high, but 90-day performance of new joiners is weak. What does this most likely mean?
o: The experience is pleasant but doesn't build role capability
Performance standards for new joiners are set much too high
The NPS survey is being completed by the wrong population
Managers are rating new joiners too harshly in early reviews
e: Satisfaction and capability are different outcomes. Strong NPS with weak performance points to content, not experience.

q: An employee on a performance improvement plan raises a grievance against the manager. What should HR do?
o: Handle it separately and decide if the plan should pause
Pause the plan automatically until the grievance closes
Continue the plan and hear the grievance once it ends
Combine both matters into a single review meeting with the manager
e: Both processes deserve fair handling. Whether to pause depends on how closely the grievance relates to the plan.

q: A company wants to cut time to productivity for new hires in 20 roles by 30%. Which approach has the most impact?
o: Role-specific capability milestones owned by managers
A longer and more detailed corporate induction programme
A buddy from another team assigned to every new joiner
Digitising all onboarding documents and joining forms
e: Productivity comes from role capability. Milestones tied to the role, owned by managers, change the outcome.

q: Leadership asks why voluntary turnover is 18% against an industry average of 12%. What is the most useful first answer?
o: Segment it by talent value, tenure and unit before acting
Turnover is clearly too high, so retention bonuses are needed
Industry averages vary widely, so the gap may not matter
Exit interview records will already show the main causes
e: Losing low performers differs from losing critical talent. Segmentation turns a headline rate into an actionable problem.

q: A hybrid working policy is planned. Staff strongly prefer flexibility, but some managers report weaker collaboration. What is the best design?
o: Team agreements inside a common framework, judged on outcomes
Three fixed office days a week for everyone in the company
Full flexibility for all, letting collaboration adjust over time
Each manager decides the rules for their own team independently
e: Team-level agreements within clear principles balance flexibility with collaboration needs and keep fairness across teams.

q: What does a structured interview mainly improve?
o: Consistency and fairness between candidates
How quickly interviews can be scheduled
The candidate's experience of the process
How many candidates can be interviewed per day
e: Same questions and scoring guides reduce bias and make candidates comparable.

q: A hiring manager wants to skip reference checks for a strong candidate to speed up the offer. What is the most balanced approach?
o: Make the offer conditional on satisfactory references
Skip the references, since the interviews went so well
Hold the offer until all the references have come back
Ask the candidate to supply written references directly
e: A conditional offer keeps the speed while keeping the control.

q: Which measure best reflects recruitment quality rather than speed?
o: New hires' performance and retention after a year
The average time it takes to fill each open vacancy
The number of applicants received per vacancy
The total cost per hire across all vacancies
e: Speed, volume and cost measure efficiency; quality of hire looks at outcomes.

q: A job description lists 15 'essential' requirements. What is the most likely effect?
o: Fewer suitable people apply, as many self-select out
Candidates arrive better prepared for the interview
The role attracts noticeably more experienced people
Hiring managers move through interviews more quickly
e: Long essential lists narrow the pool and discourage qualified candidates. Essentials should be truly essential.

q: Time to fill is rising. The longest stage is between final interview and offer approval. What should be addressed?
o: The offer approval steps and approvers' response time
The number of interview rounds in the hiring process
The sourcing channels being used for the vacancies
The overall strength of the company's employer brand
e: Fix the stage that holds the delay. Sourcing and interviews are not the bottleneck here.

q: Two final candidates score almost the same. One was referred by a senior leader. What should decide it?
o: The agreed criteria and evidence, with no weight for the referral
The referral, since the leader has seen the candidate's work
Whichever candidate is willing to accept the lower salary offer
The senior leader, who should be asked to make the final call
e: Referrals can bring candidates in, but selection must rest on criteria and evidence to stay fair.

q: A business wants a succession plan for critical roles. What comes first?
o: Identify the critical roles and what they require
Ask each manager to name their preferred successor
Run a leadership programme for every manager
Assess all high performers for future potential
e: Succession planning starts from critical roles and their requirements; successors are then assessed against them.

q: Offer acceptance fell from 85% to 60% in one quarter. What is the most useful first check?
o: Decline reasons compared with offer terms and the market
Whether recruiters are presenting offers in the right way
Whether the job descriptions are accurate and up to date
Whether the interview process has too many stages in it
e: Decline reasons point to the cause: pay, process, timing or competing offers.

q: A workforce plan shows a need for 40 data analysts in two years. The internal pipeline can supply 10. Which strategy is most realistic?
o: A phased mix of reskilling, targeted hiring and partners
Hire all 30 externally in year one to be fully ready
Rely only on reskilling, since it is the lowest-cost option
Outsource all of the analyst work to a single vendor
e: Build, buy and borrow together reduce risk and cost. One lever rarely closes a gap this size in time.

q: Assessment centre scores predict performance well for most roles but poorly for sales. What should be done?
o: Revalidate the sales criteria against what drives success
Stop using assessment centres for all roles in the company
Give interviews more weight than the centre for sales roles
Keep the current assessment, since it works for most roles
e: Poor prediction for one job family means the criteria don't measure what matters there.

q: A 9-box review rates 40% of employees as 'high potential'. What is the main problem?
o: Potential isn't differentiated, so it can't guide investment
Too many employees will now expect a promotion this year
Managers are being too generous with performance ratings
The company will need a far larger development budget
e: A label applied to 40% has lost its meaning. Calibration is needed so potential guides real decisions.

q: A role is hard to fill, and the hiring manager wants to pay 25% above the range. What should HR assess first?
o: Whether the role is scoped and graded right, and market data
Whether the department budget can absorb the higher salary
Whether other team members are likely to find out about it
Whether the preferred candidate would accept a lower figure
e: Hard-to-fill roles are often mis-scoped or mis-graded. Fixing the cause avoids distorting the structure.

q: Internal candidates fill only 15% of senior roles. Leaders say internal talent isn't ready. What is the best response?
o: Examine readiness data and development investment, then set targets
Accept the view, since leaders know the internal candidates best
Require at least one internal candidate on every senior shortlist
Introduce a fixed quota of senior promotions for internal staff
e: Low internal fill may reflect underinvestment rather than lack of talent. Data and plans address the cause; quotas alone don't.

q: A selection test has a 60% pass rate for one group and 36% for another. Using the four-fifths guideline, what should you conclude?
o: The ratio is 0.6, indicating possible adverse impact
The 24-point difference is within normal variation
The ratio is 1.67, so there's no adverse impact at all
Adverse impact needs a much larger sample to judge
e: 36 ÷ 60 = 0.6, which is below 0.8, so possible adverse impact should be investigated.

q: An employer brand campaign raised applications 70%, but hires per vacancy didn't change and screening time doubled. What happened?
o: Volume rose without better targeting of suitable people
The campaign worked and recruiters now need more capacity
The screening criteria have become far too strict to pass
Hiring managers are slower at reviewing their shortlists
e: More applicants without more hires means lower relevance. Targeting quality matters more than volume.

q: The CEO wants a 'talent density' strategy: fewer, higher-paid people. What is the most important prerequisite?
o: Agreed definitions of high performance and critical roles
A significantly larger compensation budget for top talent
A forced-distribution performance rating system across all teams
A redundancy programme for current low performers
e: Without agreed definitions of performance and critical roles, the strategy becomes arbitrary pay inflation.

q: A workforce plan assumes 20% productivity gains from automation within two years. How should HR treat this?
o: Plan scenarios and tie headcount moves to realised gains
Plan headcount reductions now based on the assumption
Ignore the assumption until the automation is fully live and stable
Ask the technology vendors to confirm the expected gains
e: Uncertain assumptions call for scenarios and trigger points, not irreversible early decisions.

q: A company drops degree requirements for skills-based hiring. What is the biggest risk if it's done badly?
o: Without valid skills tests, informal judgement takes over
Candidates who hold degrees will stop applying altogether
Salary costs will rise across the whole organisation
The volume of applications per vacancy will fall sharply
e: Removing degrees only helps if valid skills evidence replaces them. Otherwise bias returns through other proxies.

q: An employee raises a complaint against their manager and asks HR to keep it confidential. What should HR say?
o: Sharing will be need-to-know, but full secrecy can't be promised
It will stay completely confidential in all circumstances
HR has to inform the manager straight away as a matter of process
HR can only act on the complaint if it is made anonymously
e: Absolute confidentiality can't be promised if the complaint needs investigating. Honest limits build trust.

q: What is the first step in a fair disciplinary process?
o: A reasonable investigation to establish the facts
A written warning issued to the employee concerned
Suspension of the employee pending the final outcome
A recommended sanction from the employee's manager
e: A fair process starts with facts. Sanctions or suspension before investigation pre-judge the outcome.

q: A team member tells HR informally that a colleague is being bullied but doesn't want to be named. What should HR do?
o: Act on the concern without exposing who raised it
Wait for the affected colleague to complain directly
Ask the reporter to submit a formal written complaint
Tell the alleged bully's manager about it immediately
e: Concerns can be acted on without a formal complaint. Waiting can let harm continue.

q: Why should investigation meetings be documented?
o: To keep an accurate record that supports a fair decision
To show the employee the record as evidence of misconduct
To prove to auditors that the meeting actually took place
To let the manager review the notes before deciding
e: Accurate notes support fairness and defensibility.

q: A witness will only speak if their statement isn't shared with the accused employee. What is the best approach?
o: Explain the substance may be shared, anonymised where fair
Agree to full anonymity so that the evidence is obtained
Proceed with the investigation without this witness's account
Insist on a signed statement that will be shared in full
e: The accused must be able to respond to the evidence. Anonymised summaries can protect witnesses while keeping the process fair.

q: A manager wants to dismiss for poor performance, but there are no records of feedback or support. What should HR advise?
o: Start a documented process with clear expectations first
Go ahead with dismissal, as the performance gap is obvious
Ask the manager to write up past feedback notes, dated back
Move the employee to a different team instead of dismissal
e: Dismissal without evidence of a fair process is risky; backdated records would be dishonest.

q: Two employees give opposite accounts of an incident with no witnesses. How should the investigator decide?
o: On the balance of probabilities, with reasons given
Conclude nothing can be proven and close the case
Prefer the account of the more senior employee
Escalate the matter to the CEO for a final decision
e: Workplace investigations generally decide on the balance of probabilities with reasoned findings, not on rank or by default.

q: An employee raises a grievance two days after receiving a warning. What should HR consider first?
o: Whether it is really about the warning, i.e. an appeal
Treat the grievance as retaliation and decline to hear it
Withdraw the warning until the grievance has been closed
Add the grievance to the employee's disciplinary record
e: The link decides the route. Treating it as retaliation without review is unfair; automatic withdrawal is unnecessary.

q: A harassment allegation is found 'not proven', but team relationships have broken down. What is the best next step?
o: Close it with reasons and support rebuilding relationships
Move the employee who complained to a different team
Discipline both employees for their part in the conflict
Reopen the investigation to look for further evidence
e: Not proven doesn't mean false. Repairing relationships is a separate task, and moving the complainant can look like a penalty.

q: A junior employee accuses a senior leader of misconduct. Who should investigate?
o: Someone senior and independent of the leader's line
The leader's own manager, who knows the context
The HR business partner who supports the leader's team
The junior employee's manager, who saw the impact
e: Independence and perceived fairness matter most when the power difference is large. An external investigator may be appropriate.

q: An employee has frequent short absences, each covered by a medical certificate, and output is suffering. What is the best approach?
o: A supportive meeting on causes, adjustments and review
Disciplinary action for excessive absence from work
No action, since every absence is medically certified
A request for the employee's full medical history and records
e: Certified absences still need managing. A supportive, structured approach respects health and business needs.

q: A manager makes a discriminatory joke in a team meeting. No one complains. What should HR do?
o: Address it with the manager and consider the team impact
Take no action unless and until somebody files a complaint
Send a company-wide reminder about respectful behaviour
Note it on file and act only if it happens a second time
e: Employers should act on known inappropriate behaviour. Lack of a complaint can reflect fear, not acceptance.

q: A whistleblowing report alleging procurement fraud by a director reaches HR first. What should HR do?
o: Route it through the protected whistleblowing channel
Open an HR investigation into the director's conduct
Tell the director so they can respond to the claims
Ask the reporter for more evidence before any action
e: Whistleblowing needs a protected, independent route. Alerting the subject or investigating outside the process risks the evidence and the reporter.

q: A manager wants to dismiss for a first minor offence. Similar past cases received written warnings. What is the main risk?
o: Inconsistent sanctions make the decision unfair
The employee may appeal against the dismissal
Colleagues may raise complaints about the manager
The investigation report may be challenged
e: Consistency across similar cases is a core test of fairness; an appeal is a channel, not the underlying risk.

q: An employee covertly recorded a disciplinary meeting and submits it in an appeal. What should HR consider?
o: Its relevance to fairness, with the recording handled separately
Reject it automatically because it was made without consent
Dismiss the employee for breach of trust before the appeal
Accept it as conclusive evidence about what happened
e: Relevance to fairness matters. How the recording was made is a separate question under policy and applicable law.

q: After a restructure, one unit's engagement fell sharply and grievances tripled. What should HR prioritise?
o: Diagnose local drivers with the unit and act visibly
Launch a company-wide wellbeing programme
Replace the unit's whole leadership team quickly
Wait for the next survey to confirm the trend
e: Local, diagnosed action with clear owners addresses the cause. Generic programmes and waiting rarely restore trust.

q: Complaints show a valued high performer repeatedly mistreats junior staff. Leadership is reluctant to act. What is the strongest argument?
o: The full cost: attrition, legal risk and the cultural signal
Company policy requires action regardless of performance
The person may not really be a high performer after all
Other employees will eventually complain about it publicly
e: Leaders respond to total impact. Quantified people and legal costs, plus the cultural signal, make the case beyond policy.

q: A company wants mandatory mediation before any formal grievance. What is the main risk?
o: It can deter complaints and suits power-imbalance cases poorly
Training enough qualified internal mediators will be very expensive
Managers may not turn up to the scheduled mediation sessions
Mediated agreements are not legally binding on either side
e: Mediation works best when voluntary and appropriate. Making it mandatory can silence serious concerns.

q: Two reports show different headcount for the same date. What is the most likely reason?
o: They define headcount differently, e.g. contractors
One of the two reports contains a formula error
The data was extracted at different times of day
One report runs on a newer version of the HRIS
e: Definitional differences are the most common cause of conflicting headcount. Agreeing definitions comes first.

q: What is an 'effective date' in an HR system?
o: The date from which a change applies
The date the manager approved the change
The date the employee was told of it
The date the record was last edited
e: Effective dating lets systems show history correctly and drive payroll from the right date.

q: Which field is the best unique identifier for employee records across HR systems?
o: A permanent system-generated employee number
The employee's full name as on their passport
The employee's corporate email address
The employee's national identity number
e: Names change, emails get reused and IDs can be sensitive or changed. A permanent internal key is safest.

q: A dashboard shows average salary rose 8% while no one received a pay rise. What could explain it?
o: A shift in workforce mix through joiners and leavers
A data error introduced by the payroll system
Automatic inflation adjustments in the system
The dashboard using the wrong currency setting
e: Averages move with composition. Mix effects are common and need to be checked before assuming an error.

q: A turnover dashboard counts internal transfers as leavers. What is the effect?
o: Turnover is overstated and may be misdiagnosed
Turnover is understated because transfers stay in the company
The dashboard will show fewer new joiners than it should
There is no real effect if transfers are only a small number
e: Transfers are not exits from the organisation. Counting them inflates turnover, especially in units with high mobility.

q: Managers say an engagement survey result for a team of 4 should be shown separately. What is the main concern?
o: Individual answers could be identified in a group that small
Samples below ten are always statistically invalid to report
The team will score lower than larger teams on average
Managers will spend far too long on very small results
e: A minimum reporting group protects anonymity, which keeps future responses honest.

q: You are asked whether training caused higher performance, based on data showing trained employees score better. What is the main issue?
o: Those selected for training may already have been stronger
The sample size is probably too small to draw a conclusion
Performance ratings are too subjective to be used at all
The analysis leaves out the cost of the training programme
e: Correlation doesn't show causation. A comparison group or pre/post measure is needed.

q: An HRIS upgrade requires data migration. Which step most reduces the risk of bad data in the new system?
o: Cleanse and reconcile before load, then validate samples
Migrate everything and fix errors as users report them
Migrate only active employees to reduce the data volume
Freeze all HR changes for three months before migration
e: Data quality issues migrate with the data. Pre-migration cleansing and post-load validation are the core controls.

q: Attrition is 20% in Unit A and 10% in Unit B. Unit A has 30 people and Unit B has 600. What should you note before comparing?
o: Unit A's rate rests on about six leavers, so it is volatile
Unit A clearly has a retention problem that needs urgent action
Unit B's rate is more worrying because of its much larger size
The two rates can't be compared at all because of the size gap
e: Small populations create unstable rates. A few leavers move the percentage a lot.

q: The CHRO wants to predict which employees are likely to resign. What is the most important ethical safeguard?
o: Use it to improve conditions, never to penalise individuals
Make sure the model is more than 90% accurate before use
Tell every employee their own individual flight-risk score
Include as many personal data fields as possible in it
e: Flight-risk models can lead to unfair treatment. Purpose limits and governance matter more than accuracy alone.

q: Overall, women have higher promotion rates than men in a company. In every department, men have higher rates. What explains this?
o: Women are concentrated in departments that promote more
A calculation error somewhere in the department figures
Promotion rates in small departments are too unreliable
Company-level data is more reliable than department data
e: Aggregation across groups with different base rates can reverse a pattern. Department-level comparison is the relevant one here.

q: A manager asks for a report of employees with the most sick days to 'see who is abusing leave'. What should HR do?
o: Share absence patterns and support policy-based conversations
Provide the list of employees ranked by number of sick days
Refuse entirely, since all sick leave data is confidential
Provide the ranked list with employee names removed from it
e: Health-related data needs proportionate use. Ranking employees invites unfair assumptions.

q: An engagement score rose from 68 to 71. The response rate fell from 82% to 55%. How should you report it?
o: Flag that the rise may reflect who chose to respond
Report a three-point improvement in engagement this year
Report a fall in engagement because fewer people responded
Exclude the result until the response rate recovers again
e: Lower participation can bias results toward more engaged staff. Transparency about the limitation is essential.

q: You build a model that predicts high performers using hiring data. It weights postcode heavily. What is the concern?
o: Postcode can act as a proxy for protected characteristics
Postcode data changes too often to be useful in a model
The model will become too complex to explain to anyone
Employees may move house soon after they have been hired
e: Seemingly neutral variables can encode bias. Proxies must be tested and removed if unjustified.

q: An HR data warehouse has three different 'department' fields from different systems. Analysts choose different ones. What is the lasting fix?
o: One governed hierarchy with an owner, mapped to all systems
Train every analyst on which of the three fields to use
Delete two of the fields and keep the most complete one
Use whichever field happens to match the finance reports
e: Master data needs a single definition and owner. Training and ad hoc choices don't stop divergence.

q: Leadership wants one 'people health' KPI for the board. What is the strongest design?
o: A few defined leading and lagging indicators tied to strategy
A single composite index that weights all of the HR metrics
Voluntary turnover alone, since it is easy for all to understand
The engagement score alone, since it predicts most outcomes
e: A single number hides trade-offs. A few defined indicators linked to strategy inform decisions better.

q: A people analytics team produces many dashboards, but leaders rarely change decisions. What is the most likely issue?
o: The analysis starts from data, not from leaders' decisions
The dashboards are not visually appealing enough for leaders to use
Leaders lack the data literacy to read the dashboards
The data is not refreshed often enough to be trusted
e: Impact comes from answering decision-relevant questions. Data-led outputs often miss them.

q: A manager asks HR to 'run a team-building event' because the team is not working well together. What should an HR business partner do first?
o: Explore what is really going wrong before agreeing a fix
Book the event, since the manager knows the team best of all
Suggest a personality assessment for the whole team
Recommend the manager attends a leadership course
e: Good partnering diagnoses the problem before prescribing a solution.

q: What best describes an HR business partner's role?
o: Aligning people decisions with business goals
Processing HR transactions for a business unit
Representing employees in disputes with management
Enforcing HR policies across the whole business
e: HRBPs advise and align. Transactions and enforcement sit elsewhere in a mature model.

q: A leader asks for an urgent restructure proposal by tomorrow. What should an HRBP clarify first?
o: The business problem the restructure must solve
The budget available for any redundancy costs
Which employees the leader wants to keep on
The template HR uses for restructure papers
e: Structure follows purpose. Without the objective, the proposal may solve the wrong problem.

q: A business leader rejects an HR policy as 'too slow'. What is the most effective HRBP response?
o: Find the specific pain point and a compliant way to meet it
Explain that the policy must be followed in every case
Grant an exception so that the leader stays satisfied
Escalate the issue to the HR director for a decision
e: Partnering means solving within the boundaries, not defending the process or bypassing it.

q: Which is the best evidence that an HR initiative created business value?
o: A measurable change in the business outcome it targeted
High participation and satisfaction scores from employees
Positive feedback from the senior leadership team
Delivery of the initiative on time and within budget
e: Participation and delivery measure activity. Value shows in the outcome targeted.

q: Two business leaders want the same scarce talent budget. How should an HRBP help?
o: Frame options against priorities so leaders decide on trade-offs
Split the budget equally between the two business leaders' units
Give the budget to whichever leader's request is most urgent
Decide based on which of the two units has higher attrition
e: HR facilitates a priority-based decision. Equal splits and urgency rarely reflect strategy.

q: A CEO wants to adopt a competitor's unlimited leave policy. What is the strongest HR advice?
o: Test fit with culture and workload; it can reduce leave taken
Adopt it now, since it will clearly help attract new talent
Reject it, since it is far too risky to manage in practice
Pilot it in every department at once to get quick results
e: Policies don't transplant automatically. Context and second-order effects decide success.

q: Leaders keep escalating routine people decisions to HR. What should an HR leader do?
o: Clarify decision rights and build managers' capability
Take the decisions to keep the business moving quickly
Refuse escalations and send managers back to the policy
Add more HR staff to handle the volume of escalations
e: Escalation habits come from unclear authority or low capability. Fixing both moves decisions to the right level.

q: An organisational design proposal adds two management layers to 'create career paths'. What is the main concern?
o: Extra layers slow decisions and add cost for little gain
Many employees may not actually want to become managers
Each new role will need a new job description written
Managers' salaries are higher than individual contributors'
e: Structure should serve work. Layers added for progression often create bureaucracy.

q: A business is about to expand into a new market. When should HR be involved?
o: At the planning stage, to shape the key assumptions
After the decision is made, to recruit the new team
When the first hires for the new market are needed
Only if the new market has complex labour laws
e: Early HR involvement shapes feasibility and cost, not just execution.

q: Engagement is high but productivity is flat. Leadership asks HR why. What is the most insightful line of enquiry?
o: Whether goals, decision rights and work design enable output
Whether engagement is being measured incorrectly by the survey
Whether productivity will simply follow engagement after a delay
Whether employees are engaged but lack the necessary skills
e: Engaged people can still be blocked by unclear goals, poor processes or structure.

q: A change programme is on schedule, but adoption of the new way of working is low. What is the most likely gap?
o: Line managers aren't equipped or accountable to lead it
Communications about the change were not frequent enough
The training sessions provided were too short to be useful
Employees are generally resistant to all kinds of change
e: Adoption depends heavily on line managers. Communications and training alone rarely shift behaviour.

q: The executive team disagrees on whether to centralise HR. What should the CHRO bring to the discussion?
o: Explicit criteria, options assessed against them, and a view
A benchmark of what similar companies in the sector have done
A preferred option together with a detailed implementation plan
A survey of HR staff asking which model they would prefer
e: Decision quality improves with explicit criteria and options. Benchmarks and preferences alone don't resolve disagreement.

q: A strong leader is promoted but their new team's engagement drops 20 points in six months. What should HR do?
o: Targeted feedback and coaching on specific behaviours
Wait for the team to adjust to the new leader's style
Move the leader back into their previous role quickly
Run a team-building event for the leader's new team
e: Specific, evidence-based development addresses the cause early, before attrition follows.

q: A company's strategy shifts from growth to profitability. Which HR priority shift is most aligned?
o: Productivity and role clarity over headcount growth
Faster hiring to protect the company's market share
A richer benefits package to retain the current staff
More leadership development for every manager
e: HR priorities should mirror strategy. Profitability favours productivity and efficient capability.

q: Two years after a culture programme, values posters are everywhere but behaviour hasn't changed. What was most likely missing?
o: Rewards, promotions and consequences that match the values
More frequent communication of the values across the company
Values workshops attended by every employee in the business
A new and simpler set of values that is easier to remember
e: People follow what is rewarded and tolerated. Systems must reinforce stated values.

q: The board asks how the HR function itself will improve its effectiveness. What should anchor the plan?
o: The business outcomes HR must enable, turned into HR targets
A maturity-model benchmark of recognised HR best practice
A multi-year HR technology roadmap and investment plan
Feedback from the HR team itself on what its priorities are
e: Effectiveness is judged by contribution to business outcomes. Models and technology are means, not anchors.

q: Under UAE private-sector labour law, what is the maximum probation period?
o: 6 months
3 months
9 months
12 months
e: Probation may not exceed six months, and an employee can only be placed on probation once with the same employer.

q: How many days of paid annual leave is a private-sector employee entitled to after completing one year of service?
o: 30 calendar days
21 working days
24 calendar days
30 working days
e: The entitlement is 30 days per year after one year of service.

q: An employer wants to end an employee's employment during probation. What minimum written notice must be given?
o: 14 days
7 days
30 days
1 month
e: An employer terminating during probation must give at least 14 days' written notice.

q: Can a private-sector employer keep an employee's passport as a condition of employment?
o: No, employers may not keep employees' official documents
Yes, provided the employee signs a written consent form
Yes, but only during the probation period of the contract
Yes, where the employer has paid for the employee's visa
e: Employers are prohibited from confiscating employees' official documents.

q: What is the paid maternity leave entitlement for a private-sector employee?
o: 60 days: 45 at full pay and 15 at half pay
45 days, all of them at full pay
60 days, all of them at full pay
90 days: 60 at full pay and 30 at half pay
e: Maternity leave is 60 days, with 45 at full pay and 15 at half pay.

q: What is the gratuity rate for the first five years of continuous service?
o: 21 days of basic wage for each year
30 days of basic wage for each year
21 days of total wage for each year
15 days of basic wage for each year
e: Gratuity is 21 days' basic wage per year for the first five years, and 30 days per year after that.

q: An employee resigns after 11 months of continuous service. Are they entitled to end-of-service gratuity?
o: No, at least one year of continuous service is required
Yes, pro-rated for the 11 months at 21 days per year
Yes, but only if the full notice period is worked
Yes, but at half of the normal statutory rate
e: Entitlement starts after completing one year of continuous service.

q: How is paid sick leave structured after probation, per year of service?
o: Up to 90 days: 15 full pay, 30 half pay, 45 unpaid
Up to 45 days: 15 full pay and 30 half pay
Up to 90 days: 30 full pay, 30 half pay and 30 unpaid
Up to 60 days: 30 full pay and 30 half pay
e: Sick leave can total 90 days a year: 15 full pay, 30 half pay, 45 unpaid.

q: What is the minimum overtime rate for ordinary overtime hours outside 10 pm to 4 am?
o: Normal hourly wage plus at least 25%
Normal hourly wage plus at least 50%
Normal hourly wage with no premium
Basic hourly wage plus 100%
e: Ordinary overtime is paid at the normal hourly wage plus at least 25%; work between 10 pm and 4 am attracts at least 50% (except shift workers).

q: What range of notice period may a UAE private-sector employment contract specify?
o: Between 30 and 90 days
Between 14 and 60 days
Exactly 30 days for all employees
Between 30 and 180 days
e: The notice period must be at least 30 days and no more than 90 days.

q: Who must subscribe to the UAE involuntary loss of employment (ILOE) insurance scheme?
o: Eligible employees themselves
The employer, for all employees
Only UAE nationals in the private sector
Only employees above a salary threshold
e: ILOE subscription is an obligation on eligible employees; certain categories are exempt.

q: An employee in probation resigns to join another UAE employer. What notice must they give?
o: At least one month
At least 14 days
No notice is needed during probation
The full contractual notice period
e: Moving to another UAE employer during probation requires at least one month's notice; leaving the UAE requires at least 14 days.

q: Within how many days of contract end must end-of-service dues be paid?
o: 14 days
7 days
30 days
On the next payroll date
e: End-of-service entitlements are due within 14 days of the end of the contract.

q: An employee had 20 days of unpaid leave during their service. How does this affect gratuity?
o: The unpaid days are left out of the service period
Gratuity is reduced by 20 days' total wage
There is no effect at all, since employment continued
Gratuity uses the average wage of paid months only
e: Days of unpaid absence are not counted in the service period for gratuity.

q: Under the current law, does resigning reduce an employee's gratuity compared with termination by the employer?
o: No, the gratuity is calculated the same way
Yes, resigning before five years reduces it by one third
Yes, resigning before three years removes it entirely
Yes, unless the employee serves the full notice period
e: The reduction for resignation under the previous law no longer applies; gratuity is calculated the same way.

q: An employee's annual leave was not taken. On termination, how is unused leave generally paid?
o: As cash in lieu, calculated on the basic wage
As cash in lieu, calculated on the total wage
It is forfeited if not taken before termination
It is added to the notice period instead of paid
e: Unused leave is paid on termination, calculated on the basic wage.

q: How long after the end of employment does an employee have to bring a labour claim?
o: One year from the end of the contract
Six months from the end of the contract
Two years from the end of the contract
There is no time limit for such claims
e: Labour claims must be filed within one year of the end of the employment relationship.

q: A non-compete clause is being drafted. What is the maximum period it may restrict the employee after the contract ends?
o: Two years
One year
Six months
Three years
e: Non-compete restrictions may not exceed two years after the end of the contract and must be reasonable in scope.

q: What is the overall cap on end-of-service gratuity?
o: Two years' wage
One year's wage
Three years' wage
There is no cap
e: Total gratuity may not exceed the equivalent of two years' wage.

q: A manager wants to deduct the cost of a recruitment agency fee from a new hire's salary. What is the correct position?
o: Not permitted; recruitment costs can't be charged to the worker
Permitted if the employee agreed to it in the signed offer letter
Permitted, but only up to one month of the basic wage
Permitted if the employee leaves within the first year
e: Employers may not charge workers recruitment or employment fees.

q: An employee is required to work on their rest day and cannot be given a substitute day. What is the minimum compensation?
o: Basic wage for the day plus at least 50%
Normal daily wage with no premium
Total wage plus 25%
A substitute day within the following year
e: Without a substitute rest day, work on the rest day earns the basic wage plus at least 50%.

q: An employer wants to place a returning employee (rehired after 8 months away) on probation again. Is this allowed?
o: No, probation is allowed only once with the same employer
Yes, because a brand-new employment contract has been signed
Yes, but the probation is limited to three months
Yes, provided the employee's role has changed since
e: The law allows probation only once with the same employer.

q: A company with 60 employees uses two legal entities. HR wants to treat them as one for gratuity continuity after transfers. What is the key question?
o: Whether prior service was settled or expressly carried over
Whether both entities share the same trade licence activity
Whether the employee's job title changed when transferring
Whether the transfer took place within the same emirate
e: Continuity depends on employer identity and how prior service was settled or carried over, which should be documented.

q: An employee works 5 years 6 months, with a basic wage of AED 10,000. Which approach to the gratuity is correct?
o: 21 days × 5 years, plus 30 days × 0.5 year
21 days × 5.5 years on the daily basic wage
30 days × 5.5 years on the daily basic wage
21 days × 5 years; part-years don't count
e: The first five years accrue at 21 days, the remaining half-year at 30 days per year, and part-years count pro rata.

q: A bonus plan pays on 'company EBITDA and individual rating'. After payout, finance restates EBITDA down 4%. Payouts were 6% too high in aggregate. What should HR recommend?
o: Apply the plan's own adjustment or clawback terms
Recover the excess from every employee's next salary straight away
Leave the payouts in place, since employees acted in good faith
Reduce next year's bonus pool by 6% for everyone to offset it
e: The plan document governs restatements. If it has adjustment or clawback terms, apply them through governance; unilateral salary deductions or silent offsets are hard to defend.

q: The CFO proposes moving all allowances into basic salary to 'simplify payroll'. What is the most important consequence to quantify first?
o: The rise in entitlements calculated on basic pay
The time saved each month by processing fewer pay elements
The change in how payslips look to employees after the move
The number of employees who would prefer the simpler structure
e: Entitlements calculated on basic pay grow with it. The long-term liability, not admin time, usually decides whether this is affordable.

q: A sales commission plan led to record revenue but margins fell sharply. What design flaw is most likely?
o: Commission rewards revenue with no link to margin
The commission rate is too low to motivate the right behaviour
Payout frequency is quarterly rather than monthly for the team
Too few sales employees are eligible to join the plan each year
e: People optimise what the plan pays for. Paying on revenue alone encourages heavy discounting.

q: An HR system vendor proposes a configuration change that will fix a bug but alters how leave accrual is calculated mid-year. What should you insist on first?
o: Parallel testing on real accrual data before release
A written guarantee from the vendor that employees will not notice
Release at year-end only, with no testing needed in the meantime
An email to all staff explaining the bug before the fix goes live
e: Calculation changes need evidence on real cases before release. Guarantees and timing alone don't prove the outcome.

q: After an acquisition, the acquired company keeps its own HR policies 'for now'. Two years later, nothing has changed. What is the main risk to escalate?
o: Unequal treatment and legal exposure across the workforce
Higher licence costs for running two sets of HR system configurations
Confusion for HR staff who need to remember two sets of policies
A drop in employer brand ratings on public review sites over time
e: Long-term dual policies create inconsistent treatment and claims risk. Admin cost and confusion matter less than fairness and exposure.

q: HR is asked to cut its operating cost by 20% while keeping service levels. Which approach is most sustainable?
o: Remove failure demand and waste before cutting capacity
Reduce HR headcount by 20% and set the same service targets
Move all HR services to a lower-cost outsourced provider
Stop all HR projects until the cost target has been met
e: Cutting capacity while the same failure demand flows in degrades service. Removing waste first lowers the work, then the cost.

q: A strong performer asks for a fully remote arrangement after relocating abroad. The role is home-country based. What should HR check before anything else?
o: Tax, immigration and local-law implications of the move
Whether the manager is comfortable supervising someone remotely
Whether other team members have made similar requests before
Whether the employee will accept a pay cut for the arrangement
e: Working from another country can create tax, permanent establishment, immigration and local-law obligations. Those determine feasibility.

q: Exit data shows women leave at twice the rate of men at the point of promotion to manager. What should HR investigate first?
o: How the step up to manager is selected, supported and designed
Whether women are paid less than men at the manager grade
Whether the exit interview questions are biased in some way
Whether flexible working options are advertised clearly enough
e: The spike at a specific transition points to that transition: selection, support and role design. Pay and flexibility may contribute but are not where the signal points.

q: A team is moving to a new shift pattern. Most employees agree, but three refuse due to caring responsibilities. What is the best approach?
o: Consult each of the three and explore adjustments
Apply the new pattern to everyone, since the majority agrees
Exempt the three permanently so that the change can go ahead
Offer the three a transfer to another team on the old pattern
e: Individual circumstances need individual consultation. Majority agreement doesn't remove the duty to consider adjustments fairly.

q: Hiring managers reject 70% of shortlisted candidates that recruiters send. What is the most likely root cause?
o: The role brief wasn't properly agreed at intake
Recruiters are not sourcing from enough channels
Hiring managers are too busy to review CVs properly
The salary range is too low for the market
e: A high rejection rate at shortlist stage usually means recruiter and manager are working to different pictures of the role.

q: A successor has been 'ready in 1–2 years' for the CFO role for five years. What does this indicate about the succession process?
o: Readiness labels aren't tied to development or honest review
The successor is not interested in the role and should be replaced
The current CFO is blocking the successor from progressing
The rating scale needs more categories to show finer detail
e: A static readiness label signals a process that labels but doesn't develop or recalibrate. The individual explanations may be true, but the process should have surfaced them.

q: Leadership wants to use AI to screen CVs to reduce time to hire. What is the most important condition before go-live?
o: Testing it for adverse impact and validity on your roles
Confirming the vendor's tool is used by other large companies
Making sure the tool screens CVs faster than recruiters do
Training hiring managers to read the tool's ranking reports
e: Speed and popularity don't show fairness or validity. The tool must be tested on your roles and population before decisions rely on it.

q: During an investigation, the accused employee goes on sick leave and says they cannot attend meetings. What is the best approach?
o: Check fitness medically and offer options like written answers
Pause the investigation until the employee is fully back at work
Proceed without the employee's input, as they chose not to attend
Close the investigation, since the employee is now on sick leave
e: Indefinite pauses and proceeding without input are both risky. Checking fitness and offering alternatives keeps the process fair and moving.

q: An employee posts a complaint about the company on social media, naming their manager. What should HR consider first?
o: Both the conduct issue and any genuine concern raised
Asking the employee to delete the post within 24 hours
Starting disciplinary action for damaging the company's name
Replying publicly to correct the facts in the post
e: The post may contain a genuine grievance as well as a conduct issue. Both need assessment before any response.

q: Three separate grievances in a year name the same senior manager, each found 'not proven'. What should HR do now?
o: Review the pattern across the cases with leadership
Close the matter, since none of the grievances was upheld
Warn the employees that repeated complaints may be vexatious
Wait for a fourth grievance before taking any further action
e: Individual cases may lack proof, but a pattern is itself information. It justifies a wider look at behaviour and culture.

q: A collective dispute is building: 60 employees sign a petition about shift allowances. What is the best first response?
o: Meet representatives and set out a clear review process
Ignore the petition until employees raise individual grievances
Speak to each signatory one to one to understand their view
Agree to the demands quickly to stop the dispute from growing
e: Prompt, structured engagement with representatives de-escalates and shows the issue is taken seriously, without conceding before review.

q: An attrition model is 92% accurate. Only 8% of employees leave each year. What should you check before trusting it?
o: How well it identifies the people who actually leave
Whether the model has been trained on at least five years of data
Whether the 92% accuracy holds when you add more personal data
Whether the model runs fast enough to be refreshed every week
e: With an 8% base rate, a model that predicts 'stays' for everyone is 92% accurate. Precision and recall on leavers matter.

q: A pulse survey shows engagement in Team A dropped 12 points. Team A has 9 respondents. What is the most responsible way to act?
o: Treat it as a prompt to listen, not a confirmed trend
Escalate it to the leadership team as an urgent people risk
Ignore the result, since the team is too small to measure
Compare Team A's score with company averages for context
e: Small groups swing widely. The change is a reason to listen, not a basis for firm conclusions.

q: Leaders want monthly league tables ranking managers by team engagement. What is the main risk?
o: Managers pressuring teams, which corrupts honest data
League tables take too long to produce from survey data each month
Managers of large teams will always rank lower than small teams
Employees will stop reading engagement survey communications
e: When a measure becomes a target, people manage the measure. Public ranking invites pressure that undermines honesty.

q: A business unit leader asks HR to design a bonus to fix low collaboration between two teams. What should the HRBP explore first?
o: Whether goals or structure push the teams apart
How large the bonus needs to be to change collaboration behaviour
Which teams have used collaboration bonuses successfully before
How quickly the bonus could be approved and communicated
e: Low collaboration often comes from conflicting goals or structure. A bonus layered on top may not fix the cause.

q: The CEO wants to announce a four-day week next month to boost retention. What is the strongest HR advice?
o: Pilot it with measures for coverage, cost and compliance
Support the announcement, since retention is a top priority
Advise against it, since four-day weeks reduce productivity
Survey employees first and adopt it if most are in favour
e: A big working-time change needs evidence on coverage, cost and compliance. A measured pilot reduces the risk of a public reversal.

q: Two years into a skills-based organisation project, leaders still make decisions based on job titles. What is most likely missing?
o: Skills data used in staffing, pay and promotion decisions
A more detailed skills taxonomy with more skills defined
A new HR system that can display employee skills profiles
More communication about why skills matter to the business
e: Skills only change behaviour when decisions use them. A bigger taxonomy or system without that link changes little.
